Grand Bend sits on the southeastern shore of Lake Huron, a town of roughly 3,000 year-round residents that swells to nearly 50,000 on summer holiday weekends. Originally known as Brewster's Mills after settler Benjamin Brewster established a sawmill on the Ausable River in 1832, the community later took its name from the French-Canadian term "Aux Croches" — meaning "at the bends" — describing the river's winding path to the lake. Today it is one of southwestern Ontario's most popular beach destinations, drawing visitors from across Ontario, Michigan, and beyond.

With seasonal populations that large, the amount of waste, old furniture, and unwanted items that accumulates in Grand Bend is staggering. Cottage turnovers at the end of summer generate mountains of worn-out patio furniture, broken barbecues, and leftover building materials. Complete Junk Removal understands the rhythms of this beach town and schedules pickups to work around peak tourist traffic, narrow cottage laneways, and the short window property owners have to prepare for the next season.

Our crews are familiar with every corner of Grand Bend — from the bustling Main Street with its new streetscape and paving-stone sidewalks, to the quieter residential pockets north and south of the river. We serve the vacation communities of Southcott Pines, Oakwood Park, and Beach O' Pines, as well as properties along the Highway 21 corridor leading to the Pinery. No job is too small or too large: we haul away single items like a broken hot tub and handle full estate cleanouts with equal care.

The municipality's defining features are its extraordinary natural heritage: rare Oak Savanna ecosystems, deep fertile soils, and the biologically rich Ausable River corridor that winds through the landscape.

This mix of lakefront cottages, small-town homes, and working farms means the junk removal needs across Lambton Shores are as varied as the landscape itself. Forest, the largest settlement and commercial hub, grew up around a Grand Trunk Railway station named for the dense woodland that once surrounded it. Hickory Creek still meanders through town, and residents enjoy events like the Homemade Jam Music Festival and the Western Ontario Steam Threshers Show. content.intro:
Exeter is the commercial heart of the Municipality of South Huron, located roughly 40 kilometres north of London in Huron County. First settled in the winter of 1832 by Irish immigrants James and Jane Willis, the community grew steadily as Isaac Carling brought settlers from the Exeter and Devon regions of England. By 1873, the villages of Francistown on the north bank of the Ausable River and Exeter on the south merged to form a single municipality. Today Exeter is best known as the "Home of the White Squirrel" — not albinos, but a centuries-old genetic mutation of the Eastern Grey Squirrel that has become the town's beloved mascot, "Willis The White Wonder," featured on lampposts, garbage cans, and shop fronts along Main Street.

Exeter's heritage Main Street is a living archive of the families and businesses that built this town. The original Carling homestead, a designated historical landmark on Huron Street West, still stands, and a Heritage Walking Tour reveals how many original 19th-century commercial buildings remain recognisable today. The town was once home to the Verity Plow Company, whose foundry in what was then Francistown helped equip the farms that still define the surrounding landscape. Agriculture remains central to the local economy, and the intersection of Highway 4 and County Road 83 — the busiest crossroads in Huron County — buzzes with the traffic of a working rural hub.

For residents of Exeter and the surrounding farms and hamlets, junk accumulates in ways that are distinct from suburban life. Old farm implements, workshop scrap, and decades of stored belongings in barns and outbuildings need to go somewhere when properties change hands. Inside town, older homes along the tree-lined residential streets generate their share of renovation debris, worn-out furniture, and basement clutter. Complete Junk Removal handles all of it with the care and respect this close-knit community deserves.
content.localDetails:
Beyond Main Street, Exeter's green spaces are a source of genuine pride. MacNaughton Park, the best spot in town to glimpse one of the famous white squirrels, marks the start of the MacNaughton-Morrison Trail — an 8-kilometre, all-season path winding through the Ausable River Valley that connects to the Morrison Dam Conservation Area, the number-one-rated attraction in Exeter on travel review sites. The trail passes through a landscape of rolling farmland, woodlots, and river bluffs that captures the essence of Huron County. Annual events like the Exeter Ram Rodeo and the Huron Waves Music Festival — formerly the Bach Festival — draw visitors from well beyond the county, and the Goderich-Exeter Railway freight line still connects Exeter to Canadian National Railway service at London, Stratford, and Toronto, a reminder of the rail heritage that once made this town a vital link in southwestern Ontario's network.

Complete Junk Removal is committed to serving Exeter and South Huron with the same neighbourly reliability that defines life here. We sort every load, recycle metals, donate usable goods locally, and ensure that as little as possible ends up in landfill. Whether you are clearing out a century farmhouse, renovating a Main Street storefront, or simply need that old appliance hauled away, call us at 519-870-9136.

content.intro:
Bayfield is a heritage village on the Lake Huron shoreline in the Municipality of Bluewater, Huron County. Founded in 1832 by Dutch nobleman Baron van Tuyll van Serooskerken — who had purchased 388 acres from the Canada Company and named the settlement after British naval surveyor Admiral Henry Wolsey Bayfield — the village was designated a heritage conservation district in 1982, one of the earliest such designations in Ontario. That protected status means Bayfield's picturesque Main Street, lined with boutiques, galleries, and restaurants housed in beautifully preserved 19th-century buildings, looks much as it did a century ago.

Bayfield's artistic soul sets it apart from neighbouring communities. Where other small Ontario towns have struggled to maintain their main streets, Bayfield has attracted a thriving community of painters, sculptors, glass artists, and artisans who fill galleries like Main Street Gallery, Marten Arts Gallery, and Patina Studios. The weekly Bayfield Farmers Market, running Friday evenings from May through October, brings local produce and handmade goods to Clan Gregor Square, the leafy park at the entrance to Main Street where hundred-year-old trees are strung with lights and a cenotaph honours the community's war dead. The historic Bayfield Town Hall, built in 1882 and moved to the square in 1920, still retains its original village jail in the basement — uninhabited, of course.

For a village of this size, Bayfield generates a surprising volume of junk removal work. Heritage property renovations must navigate strict conservation guidelines, often producing materials that need careful handling. Seasonal residents returning to open their lakefront homes discover winter damage, outdated furnishings, and accumulated storage that needs clearing. Gallery owners and restaurateurs refresh their spaces between seasons. Complete Junk Removal serves them all with the discretion and attention to detail that Bayfield's character demands.
content.localDetails:
Pioneer Park, perched on a bluff at the corner of Bayfield Terrace and Tuyll Street, offers some of the finest sunset views on all of Lake Huron. A winding wooden staircase descends the bluff to a sandy beach below, and picnic tables and benches dot the manicured grounds above. The Bayfield River flows through the village to meet the lake at the marina, where pleasure craft bob in sheltered water and the river bridge frames autumn's blazing Carolinian forest colours. The 2.5-kilometre Heritage Trail begins at Clan Gregor Square and leads walkers past eight historical storyboards that tell the story of the village — from its founding through its evolution into the artistic enclave it is today. Annual traditions like the Bayfield Fair in August and Christmas in Bayfield, which includes the ceremonial lighting of the trees in Clan Gregor Square, reinforce the community bonds that keep this village vibrant year-round.

Complete Junk Removal appreciates what makes Bayfield special and works to protect it. We navigate narrow heritage streetscapes carefully, schedule pickups to avoid disrupting the tourist season, and ensure that salvageable architectural materials from heritage renovations are diverted from landfill whenever possible. Whether you need an estate cleared on a lakefront property, old furniture removed from a gallery space, or construction debris hauled from a heritage restoration project, call us at 519-870-9136.

content.intro:
Zurich is a small community in the Municipality of Bluewater, Huron County, situated about six kilometres inland from Lake Huron. Founded in 1856 by Swiss settlers whose heritage is still reflected in local architecture and place names, Zurich sits in the heart of Ontario's white bean country — the rich, fertile soils of Huron County produce thousands of tonnes of small dry beans that are processed, packaged, and shipped around the world. The village's most famous celebration, the Zurich Bean Festival, has been running since 1965 and draws visitors from across the province every fourth weekend of August.

Life in Zurich revolves around agriculture and community. The village itself is compact — a cluster of homes, churches, and small businesses along Goshen Street and Victoria Lane — but the surrounding countryside is a patchwork of productive farms, many of which have been in the same families for generations. When those families transition — whether through retirement, estate settlement, or modernisation — the volume of accumulated belongings, outdated equipment, and stored materials that needs clearing can be enormous. Barns, machine sheds, workshops, and century-old farmhouses all harbour decades of items that must be sorted, hauled, and responsibly disposed of.

Complete Junk Removal has deep experience serving agricultural communities like Zurich. We understand that farm cleanouts are not the same as a suburban garage clearing. The items are heavier, the distances are greater, and the scheduling needs to respect planting and harvest seasons. Our crews arrive with the equipment and the attitude to get the job done right, whether that means wrestling an ancient cast-iron stove out of a farmhouse cellar or loading a trailer's worth of scrap metal from a retired workshop.
content.localDetails:
The Zurich Bean Festival transforms this quiet village into a bustling celebration every August. Cruise Nite on Friday evening sends hundreds of classic cars along routes through neighbouring communities before they converge back in Zurich for music, midway rides, and fireworks at dusk. Saturday brings the renowned Wrench Benders Custom Rod and Antique Car Show, live cattle sorting, over a hundred vendor stalls along the main streets, and the festival's centrepiece — the legendary home-cooked baked bean and pork chop dinner that feeds close to 3,000 people, with proceeds supporting Huron Hospice. The festival has grown steadily since a group of community-minded residents launched it over half a century ago, and it remains the social highlight of the year for Zurich and the wider Bluewater area. Just minutes away, the All In Skatepark — Ontario's largest indoor skatepark at 40,000 square feet — hosts competitions including world championship events, adding an unexpected dimension to this otherwise pastoral corner of Huron County.

Complete Junk Removal is proud to serve Zurich and the surrounding Bluewater municipality. We sort every load to maximise recycling and donation, keeping usable items out of landfill and supporting the sustainability values of this farming community. Whether you need a single appliance removed from a village home or a comprehensive farm estate cleanout spanning multiple buildings, call us at 519-870-9136.

Incorporated as a village in 1860 and a town in 1872 under the motto "We Advance," Strathroy has been doing exactly that for more than 150 years. Today the Municipality of Strathroy-Caradoc has an estimated population of over 26,000 and is growing rapidly, attracting families and professionals who want small-town character with easy access to London's amenities.

That growth means construction, renovation, and transition — and all three generate junk. New subdivisions on the town's expanding edges produce mountains of construction offcuts, packaging, and debris. Older homes in the historic core near the Sydenham River undergo renovations that uncover decades of accumulated materials behind walls and under floorboards. Families downsizing from large properties to retirement living need comprehensive estate cleanouts. Complete Junk Removal handles all of it, providing Strathroy-Caradoc with the responsive, reliable service a growing community needs.

Our crews work throughout Strathroy and the surrounding communities of Mount Brydges, Cairngorm, Melbourne, and Longwood. We schedule around the rhythms of this municipality — early starts for commercial jobs downtown, flexible timing for residential pickups, and the capacity to handle large-scale cleanouts on rural properties where access can be challenging. Strathroy is our neighbour, and we treat every job here with the care and professionalism that neighbours deserve.
content.localDetails:
Strathroy's downtown core retains a genuine small-town Ontario charm. The heritage walking tour covers 12 historic buildings, and the Clock Tower Inn — housed in a landmark building in the heart of town — anchors a streetscape of independent shops and eateries. The Saturday summer market and seasonal night markets bring live music, food, and craft beverages to the downtown, creating a community gathering spot that draws residents from across the municipality. The Sydenham River itself is a biological treasure: one of the most species-rich watersheds in Canada, supporting over 80 fish species and 34 species of freshwater mussels within the Carolinian Life Zone. Nearby, Ska-Nah-Doht Village recreates a Haudenosaunee longhouse settlement surrounded by hiking trails and picnic areas, offering a window into the region's deep Indigenous history. Museum Strathroy-Caradoc preserves the local story with archives and exhibits spanning the town's founding to its railway era — three major rail lines once passed through the municipality — to the present day.

Strathroy's biggest annual event, the Hometown Turkey Festival — better known as Turkeyfest — runs every June, a nod to the town's connection to Cuddy Farms, historically the world's leading turkey-hatching company. Complete Junk Removal supports these community events and the families who attend them. content.intro:
St. Thomas is a city of approximately 42,000 residents in Elgin County, located just south of London on the north shore of Lake Erie's hinterland. Known as the Railway City, St. Thomas developed as a major rail junction in the 19th century — at its peak, multiple railway lines converged here, making it an ideal stop for everything from freight to circus trains. It was one such circus train that brought the legendary Jumbo the Elephant to town in 1885, where the famous African bush elephant met his tragic end at a railway classification yard. A century later, the city honoured Jumbo with a 38-ton life-size statue at the west end of Talbot Street, and the monument was later inducted into the North America Railway Hall of Fame.

St. Thomas is in the midst of a significant transformation. The announcement of Volkswagen's electric vehicle battery manufacturing plant — the company's first in North America — is bringing new investment, new residents, and new energy to a city that already boasted a diverse economic base in manufacturing, health care, and retail. A massive residential development on the former site of the St. Thomas Psychiatric Hospital aims to create over 3,500 new homes for 9,000 residents. With growth on this scale, the demand for junk removal, construction debris hauling, and property cleanout services has never been higher.

Complete Junk Removal has been serving St. Thomas through this period of change, helping homeowners, contractors, and businesses keep pace with the city's momentum. Whether you are clearing out a heritage property on Talbot Street, hauling renovation debris from a new build, or managing an estate transition in one of the surrounding Elgin County communities, our crews deliver fast, thorough, and responsible service.
content.localDetails:
St. Thomas wears its railway heritage with pride. The magnificent Canada Southern Station on Talbot Street, completed in 1873, was once one of the largest railway stations in Ontario and now houses the North America Railway Hall of Fame. An iconic railway bridge has been converted into Canada's first elevated park, offering sweeping views of the Kettle Creek Valley below. Talbot Street itself is lined with a significant collection of pre-1914 heritage buildings, including the St. Thomas Town Hall, the Elgin County Courthouse, the Carnegie Library, and the Armoury. Scattered throughout the city are eleven elephant-inspired murals — a public art trail that celebrates the Jumbo connection with creativity and humour. Waterworks Park, the city's first publicly owned green space, covers 25 acres of tended lawns, ornamental shrubbery, and over 5,000 vibrant flowers. And just 16 kilometres south, the Whistlestop Trail connects St. Thomas to the Lake Erie beach town of Port Stanley, making it easy to combine a day at the beach with the convenience of city living.

Complete Junk Removal understands that St. Thomas is a city in motion. We work alongside contractors building the city's future, help families settling into new homes dispose of packing materials and unwanted items, and assist long-time residents preparing heritage properties for sale or renovation. Every load we collect is sorted for recycling and donation — because a city investing this heavily in its future deserves a junk removal partner equally committed to responsible disposal. Call us at 519-870-9136.
